title: 11. Observability & SRE: Logging
summary: Logging is the practice of emitting immutable, time-ordered, machine-parseable records of events that happened inside a system, so that operators can reconstruct what occurred before, during, and after an incident.
objectives: What is the difference between structured and unstructured logging, and why does it matter at scale?
Explain the standard log levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL) and a policy for using each.
What is log cardinality, and why is it dangerous?
Compare head-based and tail-based log sampling. When would you use each?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Logging is the practice of emitting immutable, time-ordered, machine-parseable records of events that happened inside a system, so that operators can reconstruct what occurred before, during, and after an incident.
Every distributed system is, in essence, a sequence of decisions made under uncertainty. When a request fails at 03:14 AM, the engineer on call has no memory of what the system was doing — only the logs do. Logging is the discipline of recording the right events at the right level of detail so that reconstruction is possible without flooding storage with noise. At Netflix, which serves over 260 million subscribers across 190 countries, the structured logging pipeline ingests roughly 2 trillion events per day, and the difference between a five-minute recovery and a five-hour outage often comes down to whether the engineer could grep a single correlation ID across hundreds of microservices in seconds. Logging is therefore not "print statements for production"; it is the substrate on which every other observability practice depends.

The first decision in any logging strategy is structured versus unstructured. Unstructured logs are free-form text — `"User 42 logged in from 1.2.3.4"` — and they are convenient to write but brutal to query at scale. To find all logins from a given IP, you must run a substring match across billions of lines, which is both slow and error-prone (the IP might appear in unrelated stack traces). Structured logs are emitted as JSON objects with explicit fields: `{"ts":"2024-05-01T03:14:22Z","event":"login","user_id":42,"ip":"1.2.3.4","level":"INFO"}`. This lets a downstream aggregator index the `ip` field, build a B-tree over it, and answer the same query in milliseconds. Uber's M3 logging pipeline, which replaced a fragmented set of per-team ELK clusters in 2019, mandates structured JSON for exactly this reason: structured logs compress better, index faster, and let analysts compose queries with boolean operators on fields rather than fragile regex. The trade-off is developer friction — every new field must be declared, typed, and propagated through the pipeline.

The second decision is log levels. The canonical five are DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, and FATAL. DEBUG records internal state useful only during development (`"cache miss for key user:42"`). INFO marks normal lifecycle events (`"server started on port 8080"`, `"order 9912 completed"`). WARN flags abnormal but recoverable behavior (`"retry attempt 3/5 for upstream call"`). ERROR indicates a failed operation that needs attention but did not crash the process (`"payment gateway returned 502"`). FATAL is reserved for unrecoverable failures that force process exit (`"cannot bind to port 80, exiting"`). The discipline is rarely followed in practice: many teams log every exception as ERROR even when caught and retried, which pollutes alerting pipelines and trains engineers to ignore the channel. A useful rule of thumb is that ERROR must page a human if it fires at any non-trivial rate, and FATAL must page a human immediately. Netflix's internal "log taxonomy" goes further, requiring every ERROR to be associated with a runbook link in the log payload itself, so the engineer reading the log can click straight to remediation steps.

The third decision, often overlooked, is cardinality. Cardinality is the number of distinct values a field can take. A field like `level` has cardinality 5, which is fine. A field like `user_id` at Netflix has cardinality 260 million, which is catastrophic if it is indexed as a metric label — but in logs, high cardinality is acceptable and often desirable, because the log store is designed for full-text search rather than aggregation. The cardinality trap appears when teams try to use logs as metrics: counting log lines per `user_id` per minute creates an unbounded time series that explodes memory in any downstream metrics system. The rule is: logs are for high-cardinality events you will retrieve individually; metrics are for low-cardinality aggregates you will sum, average, or histogram across. Mixing the two is one of the most expensive mistakes a team can make — one e-commerce company reported in 2020 that a single debug log line containing a per-session UUID, accidentally parsed as a metric label, drove their Datadog bill from $40K to $1.2M in a single month before they noticed.

The fourth decision is sampling. At full fidelity, a hot microservice can emit thousands of log lines per second per instance, and across a thousand instances that is millions of lines per second — far more than any storage system can index cheaply. Head-based sampling decides at log emission time whether to keep a record, typically using a deterministic hash of the trace ID so the same request is either fully logged or fully dropped across all services. Tail-based sampling waits until the request completes, then keeps the log if the request was slow or errored, dropping fast successful ones — this preserves all the interesting logs while reducing volume by 90% or more. Netflix's pipeline uses tail-based sampling at the edge, keeping 100% of error and latency-outlier logs but only 1% of healthy ones, which gives them the rare combination of full incident visibility and a manageable bill.

The fifth decision is centralization. Modern systems collect logs with a lightweight agent (Fluent Bit, Vector, Filebeat) running on every host, which tails local log files, parses them, and ships them to a central aggregator. The aggregator stores them in an index (Elasticsearch for ELK, object storage + index for Loki, proprietary storage for Splunk) and exposes a query language (Lucene for ELK, LogQL for Loki, SPL for Splunk). Loki, popularized by Grafana Labs, made a deliberate trade-off: it does not index the full text of logs, only a small set of labels (app, env, instance), and relies on brute-force grep over compressed chunks for the rest. This is dramatically cheaper than Elasticsearch but slower for ad-hoc substring searches — a trade-off that works when you already know which service and time window to look at, which is the common case in incident response.

The real-world cautionary tale is the 2021 Facebook outage. During the six-hour DNS/BGP incident, internal logging tools were unreachable because they depended on the same broken network. Engineers had to fly to data centers with physical consoles to debug. The lesson, codified in every post-incident review since, is that logging infrastructure must be out-of-band from the system it observes — separate network, separate auth, separate failure domain — or it dies alongside the system when you need it most.

### ASCII Diagram
```
+-----------+    1. log line     +-----------+
|  App      | ----------------> | stdout /  |

+-----------+   "INFO",...}     +-----------+

                              +------+   +--------+

                              |  (Grafana)|
                              +-----------+
```

### Walkthrough
1. The application writes structured JSON logs to stdout or a local file, tagged with a correlation ID propagated from the request header.
2. A sidecar agent (Fluent Bit, Vector, Filebeat) tails the file, parses the JSON, attaches host and env metadata, and ships batches over TLS to the central aggregator.
3. The aggregator indexes a small set of labels (app, env, instance) and stores the full payload as compressed chunks in object storage or a hot index.
4. During an incident, the engineer queries the aggregator with the correlation ID and a time window; the query fan-outs across shards, returns matching log lines, and renders them in Grafana or Kibana alongside metrics and traces.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# structured_logger.py - runnable; emits JSON logs with levels + correlation IDs
import json, time, uuid, logging, sys
from contextvars import ContextVar

request_id: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("request_id", default="-")

class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def format(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> str:
        return json.dumps({
            "ts": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", time.gmtime(record.created)),
            "level": record.levelname,
            "logger": record.name,
            "msg": record.getMessage(),
            "request_id": request_id.get(),
            "func": record.funcName,
            "line": record.lineno,
        })

def build_logger(name: str) -> logging.Logger:
    log = logging.getLogger(name)
    log.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
    h = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
    h.setFormatter(JsonFormatter())
    log.handlers = [h]
    log.propagate = False
    return log

log = build_logger("orders")

def handle_order(user_id: int, sku: str):
    rid = str(uuid.uuid4())
    token = request_id.set(rid)
    try:
        log.info("order_received", extra={"user_id": user_id, "sku": sku})
        if sku == "BROKEN":
            log.warning("inventory_miss", extra={"sku": sku})
            raise RuntimeError("out of stock")
        log.info("order_completed", extra={"user_id": user_id, "sku": sku})
    except Exception as e:
        log.error("order_failed", extra={"err": str(e)}, exc_info=True)
    finally:
        request_id.reset(token)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    handle_order(42, "WIDGET-RED")
    handle_order(99, "BROKEN")
```

INFO records normal lifecycle events that an operator expects to see in steady state — server start, request received, order completed. WARN flags abnormal but recoverable behavior — retries, degraded fallback, rate-limited calls.

The decision hinges on query patterns and budget.

quiz.explanation: Head-based sampling decides at log emission time whether to keep a record, typically by hashing a trace ID deterministically so the same request is fully logged or fully dropped across all services. It is simple, stateless, and cheap, but it samples blindly — it discards 99% of errors just as readily as 99% of healthy requests.

quiz.question: How do correlation IDs (trace IDs) propagate across microservices, and why are they essential for logging?
options: Alerting on raw log substring matches is almost always wrong because it produces unactionable noise — every transient retry or expected decline fires a page.
The decision hinges on query patterns and budget.
The goal is to move logs off the boxes into a central, queryable store without rewriting applications.
A correlation ID is a unique identifier generated at the edge of the system (typically by the API gateway or first service) and propagated to every downstream service…
quiz.explanation: A correlation ID is a unique identifier generated at the edge of the system (typically by the API gateway or first service) and propagated to every downstream service via a request header like X-Request-ID or traceparent (per W3C Trace Context). Each service reads the header on entry, attaches it to every log line as a structured field, and forwards it unchanged on outbound calls.
